content.text: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Honestly, today my bookmarks are a mess — they live in different browsers, the names are whatever the page happened to be called, and I can never find anything later. So when this is done, here's what I'd want to feel different.

When I save a link, I just want to paste the address and have it sort itself out — pull in the page's title, a short description, the little site icon, maybe a picture — so I'm not typing all that by hand. And if I ever try to save something I already saved, I don't want a second copy; I'd want it to just take me to the one I already have so I can tweak it.

Then, finding things again should be the easy part. I want to search across everything — the titles, my own notes, the descriptions, the web address — without worrying about capital letters. I want to label things with my own tags and click a tag to see just those. And I'd love to stash things as "read this later" and be able to pull up just that pile when I have time, then check them off as I get through them.

I also want to keep the stuff I care about from disappearing on me — so if a page goes away later, I still have what it said saved somewhere.

That's the heart of it for me. What are you picturing so far?

Yes, that's exactly the direction — turning a pile of scattered, forgettable links into a library I actually trust and can find my way around.

A couple of things I'd add to make sure we're on the same page, since you captured the spirit well:

When I said tags, I don't just mean sticking labels on — I want it to help me while I type, suggesting tags I've already used so I don't end up with "recipe" and "recipes" and "cooking" all meaning the same thing. And searching should feel smart: I want to be able to search by a tag specifically, and combine things — like "show me anything about Rome that's either an article or a book" — not just type one word and hope.

On the reading side, "read later" is one thing, but I also picture the list itself being pleasant to skim — I should see the title, the description, and the tags right there, and clicking an item should just take me to the actual page.

And the whole thing is just for me — my own personal home base. I'm not thinking about other people logging in or sharing.

Does that all still fit what you're picturing?

I'm mostly picturing a website — something I open in my browser on my computer, since that's where I'm usually reading and collecting links anyway. It'd be nice if the page didn't look broken if I happened to pull it up on my phone, but I'm not asking for a separate phone app or anything I install. A regular site I log into and it's all there is what I have in mind.

This feels right, and I like it a lot. Pasting the link, watching it go find the details, then landing on a filled-out entry in my library — that's exactly the effortless save I was hoping for. Starting empty makes sense too.

The review step is the right idea. One thing I'd want there, though: right now I can add my own notes, but the title and description it found are just sitting there fixed. Sometimes the title a page gives itself is clunky or too long, and I'd want to tidy it up — or fix the description — right there before I save it, without having to go hunt for an edit screen afterward. So the review shouldn't just show me what it found; it should let me adjust the title and description too.

Can you make those editable at that step? Otherwise the saving flow is just what I pictured.

Yes — this is right. I changed the title and the description on the review step, saved, and the entry in my library showed my edited version, not the original. That's exactly what I wanted: it finds the details for me, but I get the final say before it lands.

The saving flow matches what I pictured. Happy with this one — what's next?

This is exactly what I hoped for. When I pasted the same link again, instead of quietly making a second copy, it told me I'd already saved that address and brought up my existing bookmark — with my old notes still on it — ready to adjust. I changed the title, saved, and I still had just the one entry, now updated. No duplicate. That's the behavior I wanted.

Using the exact web address to recognize a repeat feels like a sensible starting point, and opening the existing one right there in the save flow is good.

One small thing I'll mention so it doesn't surprise us later — I don't need it solved now: the same page can sometimes hide behind slightly different addresses, like one with a trailing slash or a bunch of tracking gibberish tacked on the end. I noticed you already shrug off a trailing slash, which is nice. I'm fine treating exact-match as the rule for now; just wanted to flag it.

This one's good. What's next?

I tried both, and they land in the same place. For everyday use I'd go with Version B — the little box right there on the page where I paste and hit Continue. Since I'm always coming here to drop in a link, having the box already sitting in front of me feels quicker and more natural than clicking a button to open a window first.

The one thing I'd ask: keep the review step B shows — where I get to see and tidy the found title and description before it actually saves. As long as I still get that moment to adjust before it lands, Version B is my pick.

That works nicely. I typed "tra", saw my existing "travel" suggestion pop up under the field, picked it, saved — and the new bookmark showed up with the travel tag on it. And I like that it's suggesting tags I've already used so I'm not accidentally spinning up "travel" and "Travel" and "trips" that all mean the same thing. That was exactly my worry.

One thing I want to make sure works, since it's really the other half of tagging for me: what happens the very first time I use a brand-new tag that isn't in the suggestions yet? Say I type "florence" and I've never used it before — nothing will match. I'd still want to be able to just add it as a new tag right there and have it stick to the bookmark (and then show up as a suggestion next time). Can you show me that case? As long as I can both pick an existing tag and create a new one, the tagging feels right.

That's the other half working just how I hoped. Typing "florence" when it's brand-new gave me a clear "Create new tag" choice, it stuck to the bookmark, and then when I started the next save and typed "flo" it was sitting right there as an existing suggestion — so I won't keep re-inventing it. 

Keeping new tags in lowercase is fine by me; that's exactly the kind of tidiness that stops me ending up with "Florence" and "florence" as two separate things. And asking me to actually pick "Create new tag" rather than silently making one the instant I type feels right — I'd rather say so on purpose.

Tagging's good. What's next?

I tried both. Version B, where all my tags sit there as little chips I can filter and click, is pleasant when I've only got a handful — but I can see that getting crowded once I've built up a lot of tags over time. Version A, where I just type and the matches drop down under the field, is the one I'd want for regular use; it stays calm no matter how many tags I've accumulated, and it's the same spot where I get the "create new tag" option when I'm typing something fresh.

So I'll go with Version A — as long as it keeps both parts: matching my existing tags as I type, and letting me create a brand-new one right there. That's my pick.

Yes — that's just what I expect. I typed ROME in capitals and it still pulled up four of the five, and when I looked at why each one matched, they were matching in different places — one in the title, one down in a personal note I'd jotted, one in the description, and one buried in the web address. That's the reassuring part for me: I don't have to remember which field I put the word in, I just type it and it looks everywhere, capital letters or not. And Clear brought all five back.

That's the broad, forgiving search I wanted. Good — what's next?

Both landed on the same three, which is the main thing. They feel pretty different to build, though.

Version B — typing Rome and then clicking the tag chips — is the friendlier one to reach for casually. But I can see its ceiling: it's an "any of these / all of these" toggle, and that's about it. The moment I want something a little more particular, it runs out of room.

Version A, where I write out "Rome in articles or books" as a sentence, looks slightly more fussy at first, but it's the one that won't box me in. Because here's the kind of thing I know I'll eventually want: "Rome, and either articles or books, but not the ones tagged travel" — grouping a couple of tags together with an "or" and then excluding another. A typed search can carry that in one line; a row of toggle chips really can't.

So I'll go with Version A. Two things I want to confirm come with it, since they're the whole reason I'm picking it: I can single out a tag specifically (not have "books" the word accidentally match a description), and I can use "and," "or," "not," and group things in parentheses. Does A handle an exclude like "not travel" and a grouped "(articles or books)" too?

That's exactly what I wanted, and the little plain-language readout under the box — "text contains Rome, and either tag articles or tag books, and exclude travel" — is genuinely reassuring, because I can double-check it did what I meant before trusting the results.

I especially like the honest example you slipped in: the "bookseller's guide" that has the word "books" sitting in its description but not as a tag got correctly left out. That's the exact distinction I was worried about — I want a tag to mean the label I stuck on, not just the word appearing somewhere. Good.

One question that comes straight out of this, since you've made "and / or / not" into special words: what happens the day I actually want to search for one of those words itself? Say I saved something with "Law and Order" in the title, and I just type that phrase — I wouldn't want it treating "and" as a command and getting confused. Is there a way for me to say "no, I mean the literal words" — like putting quotes around a phrase to search it exactly as written? If I can do that, the search is complete for me.

That completes it. Pressing Search on the quoted phrase kept only "Law and Order in the Early City" — the one where those three words sit together in that order — and correctly dropped the one that just had the same words scattered around, the one with them reversed, and the note that happened to mention law and order separately. And it spelled out that the "and" in the middle was being treated as plain text, not a command. That's precisely the escape hatch I wanted.

Keeping it case-insensitive at the same time is right too — I don't want to have to match capitals to find my own phrase.

So that rounds out search for me: broad and forgiving by default, able to single out tags, combine with and/or/not and grouping, and a way to lock an exact phrase when I need it. Happy with search. What's next?

That's the reading flow just as I pictured it. I hit "Read later" on the water-cities one and it dropped into its own pile; the "Read later" section gave me a clean, focused list of just the things I've set aside; and when I checked one off with that round button, it left the pile and the count ticked down — but back in the main Library the bookmark was still sitting there, safe. That last part matters to me: "I've read this" shouldn't mean "throw it away." It just means clear it off my to-read stack.

Having it as a standing section I can pop into whenever I've got time, rather than something I have to set up each visit, is exactly right too.

Reading workflow's good. What's next?

Both do the same thing, so this is just a taste call. I'll go with Version B — the "Mark read" button. The plain checkbox circle in A is fine, but a labeled button leaves no doubt about what it does; with just a hollow circle I'd second-guess whether I'm about to mark it done or accidentally delete it. Having the words "Mark read" right there tells me exactly what'll happen. So Version B is my pick.

Yes — this is exactly the safety net I was hoping for. I opened the article, got the "this page can't be reached anymore" notice, and the saved copy still had the whole thing: the text was all there to read, the picture came through, and it still showed who wrote it and where it was originally published. So even though the live page is gone, I haven't actually lost what mattered — the content and the "where did this come from" details are preserved.

And I like that it happens quietly on its own when I first save, rather than me having to remember to press "save a copy." That's the whole point for me — I won't think to do it in the moment, so it needs to just happen.

I'm fine that the copy is the readable article rather than a fully working live version of the site — I don't need the buttons and interactive bits, I need the words and pictures to survive. That's the right trade.

This is the fallback I want. What's next?

Both got me to the article and back fine. My preference comes down to not losing my place in the library. When I click into an article to read it, I usually want to come back and keep going down my list — so I'd rather the original open in a separate tab and leave my library sitting exactly where it was, rather than my library page being replaced and me having to find my way back to the same spot.

Whichever of these keeps my library open and undisturbed in the background is the one I want — that reads like Version B, where I pop over to the article and my library's still there waiting when I'm done. So Version B, as long as opening an article never makes me lose where I was in my list.

Both got me to my library. I'll go with Version A — the straightforward email-and-password sign-in. Since this is just my own private collection that I'll be popping into often, having to bounce out to my email, wait for a link, and come back every time I want to sign in would get tiresome fast. Typing my password and I'm straight in feels quicker and more like something I control. So Version A is my pick.

I'll go with Version B. Version A just refuses and leaves me with nothing, which would frustrate me — sites are down for a minute all the time, and if I've got a link in hand I want to get it into my library right then, while I'm thinking of it, not lose it because the page happened to hiccup. Version B lets me save the address with my own title and a note, tells me honestly that there's no saved copy yet, and — the part I really like — says it'll keep trying on its own to grab the details and a copy later. So I don't have to babysit it or remember to come back and redo it.

The one thing I'd want to be sure of, since it matters to me: that bookmark shouldn't just sit half-finished forever and silently give up. As long as it keeps retrying and fills in the page details and the saved copy once the site's reachable again — and I can still tidy the title myself in the meantime — Version B is the outcome I want.

That closes the loop just how I wanted. I changed the title to my own wording, saved it, and while it waited the bookmark was clearly marked as still trying — no pretending it was finished. Then when the page came back, the description, the site icon, and the "saved copy ready" all filled themselves in on their own, and — the crucial bit — my title stayed exactly as I'd written it. It didn't barge in and overwrite what I'd chosen with whatever the page calls itself.

That's the right balance: it does the fetching work for me automatically once it can, but it treats anything I've deliberately set as mine to keep. That completes the unreachable-page behavior for me. What's next?

Both feel right. When I ran the half-finished search, it didn't just throw up its hands or silently show me a random subset — it told me plainly what was missing ("after OR, add another condition and close the bracket") and, importantly, left my library showing exactly what it was showing before. That's the reassuring part: a typo in my search doesn't disturb what I was already looking at.

And the empty result for `tag:astronomy` — a tag I've never used — was handled honestly too: a clear "nothing matches this" rather than a blank confusing screen, with a one-click way straight back to my full library. That matters because a search turning up nothing is normal, and I shouldn't feel stuck when it happens.

So yes, both behaviors are what I'd want. What's next?

That recovery feels right. When I signed in with the wrong password, it kept my email address filled in so I didn't have to retype it — just cleared the password box for me to try again — and the message stayed general rather than announcing "that email doesn't exist" or "wrong password." I actually like that it's vague: since this is my private collection, I don't want it confirming to anyone poking at it whether they've hit a real account or not. And then "bookmarks" got me straight in.

So it's the right blend — quick and forgiving for me when I fat-finger my password, but not chatty about the details. Good. What's next?

I'll take Version B. This is the exact thing I flagged earlier — the same page arriving with a bunch of "utm" newsletter-tracking junk stuck on the end. In Version A it counted that as a brand-new page and would've made me a second copy of the Rome guide, which is precisely the clutter I'm trying to avoid. Version B saw through the tracking bits, recognized it as the one I already have, and brought up my existing bookmark to tweak instead. That's what I want.

I'm glad you were careful about how far this goes, though — I wouldn't want it getting overeager and treating every little difference in the address as throwaway. Some of what comes after the "?" genuinely points to a different page (a specific article number, a page-two, that kind of thing), and I'd be upset if it merged two genuinely different pages into one because it assumed the tail didn't matter. So as long as it's only the recognizable tracking tags it strips — the marketing "where did you come from" stuff — and it leaves meaningful address details alone, Version B is the behavior I want.

That's a nice ending for the pile. I marked the last item read, the count dropped to zero, and instead of a cold empty box I got a friendly "you're all caught up" — with the reminder that nothing was thrown away, just cleared off my to-read stack. That reassurance matters to me every time, not just once; I never want to wonder whether emptying the pile also emptied my library. And the single "Browse library" button gave me an obvious way back rather than leaving me stranded on an empty page.

So yes — right ending for the reading pile. What's next?

That validation feels right. Empty field gave me a plain "paste a web address to continue"; typing "notes from rome" — which is just words, not a link — got a clear "this doesn't look like a complete web address, try one starting with http:// or https://"; and in both cases it left what I'd typed sitting there instead of wiping it, and didn't sneakily tack anything on to make it "work." Then the real Rome address went through fine.

That's the behaviour I'd want: it only ever starts a save from a genuine web address, so I don't end up with junk entries from a stray note I pasted by mistake, but it tells me plainly what to fix rather than just refusing, and never touches my typing while it does. Good. What's next?

Before you start building, yes — this is broadly the scope we've worked through, and I'm glad it's all captured. Two everyday things jump out at me as missing, though, and they're basic enough to managing bookmarks that I'd want them in from the start rather than discovered later:

First, getting rid of one I no longer want. We've covered marking things read and saving copies, but I don't see anywhere I can just delete a bookmark for good — say I saved something by mistake, or it's gone stale and I never want to see it again. That's different from "read" or "set aside," and I'd expect a clear, deliberate way to remove it entirely.

Second, going back to fix one I already saved. I can tidy the title and tags at the moment I save, and I saw I can adjust an existing one when I re-paste its address — but what about a bookmark that's been sitting in my library for weeks and I just want to rename it, re-tag it, or fix a typo in my note? I'd want to open any saved bookmark and edit it directly, without having to re-paste the link to get at it.

If those two — deleting a bookmark, and editing an already-saved one anytime — are included alongside everything else, then go ahead and start building. Can you confirm they're in?

Both let me open any saved bookmark, change the title, tag, and note, and the card updated right there — no re-pasting the address, which is exactly what I was missing. And I like that the web address and the saved copy stay untouched; I'm only tidying my own details, not disturbing the underlying link or the preserved page.

Between the two ways in, I'll go with Version A — the plain "Edit" button sitting on the card. With Version B's little "…" menu I'd have to click it first just to discover editing is in there; the labeled button tells me straight away that this is how I fix something up. So Version A is my pick, as long as opening the editor that way still leaves the address and the saved copy alone.

Ready for the delete flow whenever you are.

I'll go with Version A — the confirmation before it happens. Since this delete is the truly permanent one — it takes the bookmark, my notes, its spot in Read later, and the saved copy all with it — I'd rather be asked "are you sure?" and stop it before it's gone than have it vanish instantly and hope I catch a little "Undo" before it disappears. With the undo approach, if I look away or the message fades, I've lost the saved copy for good with no way back. A moment's pause to confirm is the safer feel for something this final.

And I'm glad you spelled out that it clears everything tied to the bookmark on my side but never touches the actual website — that's the right boundary. Deleting my bookmark shouldn't reach out and do anything to the real page; it just removes my copy and my notes.

So Version A's confirmation is my pick. What's next?

# Development

Phase 2. Design and implement based on the Gherkin specification.

---

## Context-dependent behaviour

| Context | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| First cycle | Full design and implementation |
| Later cycles | Reflect the design of affected parts and fix the implementation |

---

## Implementation basis

Use the GWT (Gherkin) of approved scenarios as the basis for functional behaviour.
Do not arbitrarily add behaviour not included in the Gherkin.
Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
scenarios' GWT specifications. Develop the production code in `implementation/`,
separately from the exploration code in `prototypes/`.

This restriction applies to exploration code, including prototypes made in later
cycles. Later cycles may modify the existing production implementation according
to the updated approved GWT; they do not require rebuilding it from scratch.

---

## Internal information system

Accumulate the following information during implementation. Keep the format
lightweight, but at a level that enables impact analysis in later cycles.

### Design-decision record
What was decided, why, and which alternatives were dropped.
Notes for understanding the structure after context is reset.

### Scenario-code mapping
Which scenario (SCN-NNN) corresponds to which code.
The basis for judging the impact scope on a change request.

### Tests
Create tests together with the implementation.
Include both Gherkin-based acceptance tests and internal unit/integration tests.

---

## Sufficiency criteria

The internal information system is sufficient when it meets both of:
- A level that enables impact analysis in later cycles
- A level from which, if the user requests traditional artifacts (design
  documents, test plans, etc.), they can be generated and provided

---

## Transition to Phase 3

When implementation and test creation are complete, switch to Phase 3
(verification).

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [20]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/home/node/.codex/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- plugin-creator: Create and scaffold plugin directories for Codex with a required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, optional plugin folders/files, valid manifest defaults, and personal-marketplace entries by default. Use when Codex needs to create a new personal plugin, add optional plugin structure, generate or update marketplace entries for plugin ordering and availability metadata, or update an existing local plugin during development with the CLI-driven cachebuster and reinstall flow. (file: r0/plugin-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)

---

| Context | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| First cycle | Verify against all scenarios |
| Later cycles | Regression-verify updated scenarios + affected existing scenarios |

### Gherkin-based acceptance tests
Run against the Gherkin of approved scenarios.
Every Scenario's Given/When/Then must pass.

### Internal tests
Run the unit/integration tests created alongside the implementation in Phase 2.

---

### Gherkin acceptance-test failure
The implementation does not match the approved behaviour.
-> Return to Phase 2 and fix the implementation.
-> Do not change the scenario.

### Internal test failure
An internal quality problem of the implementation.
-> Return to Phase 2 and fix the implementation.

---

## Transition to Phase 4

When all tests pass, switch to Phase 4 (acceptance).

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-001.md
Scenario ID: SCN-001
Title: Save a new bookmark with discovered and editable page details
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
From an empty library, the client can paste a web address into a save field that is already visible on the library page and continue. The site gathers the page title, description, and site icon, then presents the discovered details for review. The client can edit the discovered title and description and add optional personal notes before saving. Saving creates one library entry that uses the client's edited values.

## Gherkin
Feature: Save bookmarks

  Scenario: Save a bookmark using discovered page details
    Given the personal library is empty
    When the client pastes a valid web address into the save field on the library page
    And continues
    Then the discovered title, description, and site icon are presented for review
    And the client can add optional personal notes

  Scenario: Adjust discovered details before saving
    Given discovered page details are being reviewed
    When the client changes the title and description
    And saves the bookmark
    Then one bookmark is added to the library
    And its title and description match the client's edited values

## Assumptions
- The client is already inside their private personal library.
- The submitted address is valid and reachable, and page details are available.
- The library has no bookmarks before this flow begins.
- Personal notes are optional and do not replace the page description.
- The web-address field remains visible on the library page so saving does not require opening a separate window first.
- Continuing from the web-address field always leads to the editable review step before the bookmark is saved.

## Related scenarios
- None

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-002.md

Title: Reuse an existing bookmark when the same address is saved again
Type: Edge Case
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-002

## Approved behaviour
When the client tries to save an address that is already in the library, the site explains that it has already been saved and opens the existing bookmark within the save flow. Existing details, including personal notes, remain available for adjustment. Saving changes updates that bookmark and leaves exactly one copy in the library.

    Given one bookmark already exists for a web address
    And that bookmark has personal notes

    And the existing bookmark opens for editing with its notes intact

  Scenario: Update the bookmark found during duplicate detection
    Given the existing bookmark has opened during the save flow
    When the client changes its title and saves the changes
    Then the existing bookmark has the changed title
    And the library still contains exactly one bookmark for the address

## Assumptions
- Comparison is case-insensitive and ignores a single trailing slash.
- Addresses that differ in other ways, including tracking query information, are distinct for the approved behaviour.
- Editing the existing bookmark happens inside the save flow.

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-003.md

Title: Reuse an existing tag while saving a bookmark
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-003

## Assumptions
- Tag suggestions are shown in a matching dropdown beneath the tag field while the client types; tags are not displayed as a permanently expanded tray.

- Tags are visible on bookmark entries in the library.

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-006.md

Title: Combine broad text with either of two specific tags
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-006
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
The client can express a combined search in one typed request. ## Assumptions
- The combined search is written in one search field rather than assembled from a permanently visible tray of tag toggles.

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-007.md
Scenario ID: SCN-007
Title: Group and exclude exact tag criteria in a typed search
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-007
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
The client can write a single search expression using AND, OR, NOT, and parentheses. A `tag:name` criterion targets an exact tag rather than the same word in another bookmark field. Parentheses group alternatives, and NOT excludes matching bookmarks. The site shows a plain-language interpretation of the expression so the client can verify what it understood before trusting the results.

## Gherkin
Feature: Express precise bookmark searches

  Scenario: Group tag alternatives and exclude another tag
    Given the library contains bookmarks with varied searchable text and tags
    When the client searches for "Rome AND (tag:articles OR tag:books) AND NOT tag:travel"
    Then every result broadly matches "Rome"
    And every result has the exact tag "articles" or the exact tag "books"
    And no result has the exact tag "travel"

  Scenario: Do not confuse ordinary text with a tag criterion
    Given a bookmark contains the word "books" in its description
    But it does not have the tag "books"
    When the client searches using "tag:books"
    Then that bookmark is not included because of its description text

  Scenario: Show how a precise search was understood
    Given the client entered a search containing grouped, alternative, and excluded criteria
    When the search is applied
    Then a plain-language interpretation identifies the broad text, exact tags, grouping, and exclusion

## Assumptions
- `tag:name` is the notation for targeting a tag exactly.
- AND, OR, and NOT are available as search operators.
- Parentheses determine grouping.
- Search expressions and tag names are interpreted without regard to capitalization.

- SCN-005

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-009.md

Type: Happy Path

Approval session: SESSION-009
Approval cycle: 1

The client can add an existing bookmark to Read later with one action from its library card. Read later is a persistent library section with a count and a focused list containing only queued bookmarks. The client can mark a queued bookmark as read; it immediately leaves the pile and the count decreases, while the underlying bookmark remains safely available in the main library.

## Gherkin
Feature: Manage a read-later pile

  Scenario: Add a bookmark to Read later
    Given a bookmark is in the library and not in Read later
    When the client adds it to Read later from its library card
    Then the bookmark is included in the Read later section
    And the Read later count increases

  Scenario: View only queued bookmarks
    Given some library bookmarks are in Read later and others are not
    When the client opens the persistent Read later section
    Then only queued bookmarks are shown

    When the client marks it as read

    And the Read later count decreases

- Read later is a standing library section rather than a temporary filter that must be rebuilt.

FILE ../context/scenarios/SCN-013.md
Scenario ID: SCN-013
Title: Save an unreachable page and complete it automatically later
Type: Error Case
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-013
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
If a submitted page cannot be reached, the client can still save its address with a manually supplied title and notes. The bookmark clearly remains in a waiting state and honestly states that no saved copy exists yet. Keepwell retries automatically without requiring the client to babysit it. When the page becomes reachable, the site icon, description, and readable saved copy are filled in automatically. Any field the client deliberately edited, especially the title, is preserved rather than overwritten by recovered page details.

## Gherkin
Feature: Recover incomplete bookmark captures

  Scenario: Save an unreachable page in a waiting state
    Given a submitted page cannot be reached
    When the client supplies a title and saves it anyway
    Then the address and client-supplied details are saved as a bookmark
    And the bookmark clearly states that page details and a saved copy are still pending
    And automatic capture retries remain scheduled

  Scenario: Complete a bookmark after its page recovers
    Given an incomplete bookmark is waiting for automatic capture
    And the client deliberately edited its title
    When a later retry reaches the page
    Then the description and site icon are filled in
    And a readable saved copy becomes ready
    But the client-edited title remains unchanged

## Assumptions
- Capture retries continue automatically until successful rather than silently giving up.
- A waiting bookmark remains visibly distinguishable from a fully captured bookmark.
- Recovered details fill missing values but never overwrite fields deliberately edited by the client.

    Given the client is viewing a set of library bookmarks

    And the previously visible bookmarks remain unchanged

    Given no bookmark has the tag "astronomy"
    When the client searches for "tag:astronomy"
    Then a clear no-matches state is shown
    And the client can clear the search with one action
    When the client clears it
    Then the full library is visible again

## Approved behaviour
When sign-in fails, the client remains signed out and sees a deliberately general message that does not reveal whether the email or password was wrong.     Given a failed sign-in message is visible
    When the client enters the correct password and signs in again
    Then their private library opens

- Sign-in errors never distinguish an unknown email from an incorrect password.
- Retaining the email is acceptable, but retaining an incorrect password is not.

Title: Ignore recognized tracking parameters during duplicate detection
Type: Edge Case
Approval status: approved

## Approved behaviour
When a submitted address differs from a saved address only by recognized marketing or referral tracking parameters, the site treats it as the same bookmark and opens the existing entry for editing rather than creating a duplicate.     Given two addresses differ by a parameter that is not recognized as tracking
    When the client saves both addresses
    Then they remain eligible to be stored as distinct bookmarks

- Only a maintained set of recognized marketing and referral parameters is ignored.
- Parameters with unknown or content-bearing meaning are preserved.
- Ignored tracking parameters do not replace the stored original address.

Every saved bookmark has a plainly labelled Edit button on its library card. Scenario ID: SCN-020
Title: Permanently delete a bookmark after explicit confirmation
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-020
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
Every bookmark has a clear Delete action. Selecting it does not immediately remove anything; a confirmation names the bookmark and explains that permanent deletion removes the bookmark, personal notes, Read later membership, and saved readable copy. Only an explicit "Delete permanently" action completes removal. Deletion affects only the client's stored material and never the original website.

## Gherkin
Feature: Permanently delete bookmarks

  Scenario: Explain the full effect before permanent deletion
    Given a bookmark has notes, Read later membership, and a saved readable copy
    When the client selects Delete
    Then a confirmation explains that all of those stored items will be removed
    And nothing has been deleted yet

  Scenario: Confirm permanent deletion
    Given the permanent-delete confirmation is open
    When the client selects "Delete permanently"
    Then the bookmark is removed from the library
    And its personal notes are removed
    And its Read later membership is removed
    And its saved readable copy is removed
    But the original website is unaffected

## Assumptions
- Permanent deletion requires confirmation before any data is removed.
- Deletion applies to all client-owned data attached to that bookmark.
- The confirmation safeguard is preferred to a time-limited undo notification.

Feature: Cancel bookmark management actions safely

    And the unsaved title change is discarded
    And every stored bookmark detail remains unchanged

  Scenario: Cancel permanent deletion
    Given the permanent-delete confirmation is open for a bookmark
    When the client cancels deletion
    Then the confirmation closes
    And the bookmark remains in the library
    And its title, notes, tags, Read later membership, and saved copy remain unchanged

## Assumptions
- Cancel means discard, with no draft retained.
- No deletion side effect occurs before explicit permanent confirmation.

item.stdout:
# Acceptance

Phase 4. Present the result to the user and obtain acceptance confirmation.

---

## Acceptance procedure

### Presenting the result

Present the implemented software to the client and report that verification
against the approved scenarios' GWT specifications and the internal tests has
passed. Summarise the verification outcome in plain language and provide access
to the implemented software.

For the first cycle, the report covers all approved scenarios. For later cycles,
it covers the changed scenarios and affected existing scenarios.

### Acceptance confirmation

Ask the client to accept the implemented software as a whole on the basis of
the approved behaviour and the verification report. Acceptance completes the
development work for the cycle.

### Handling client requests

Use the requirement scenarios approved during Phase 1 as the baseline. Classify
each request by whether fulfilling it changes that baseline:

- Implementation error: the implementation does not satisfy an approved
  scenario. Return to Phase 2, fix the implementation, repeat verification in
  Phase 3, and request acceptance again. Preserve the approved scenario.
- Requirement change or addition: fulfilling the request requires changing an
  approved scenario or adding a scenario. Record the request for the next cycle
  in context/session-log.md, retaining the current approved scenarios.

Explain the classification using the previously approved behaviour in plain
language. If the client's request is unclear, clarify whether the software fails
to perform that behaviour or the desired behaviour has changed. Keep requirement
exploration within Phase 1 of the cycle that will address the change.

After recording a requirement change or addition, ask for acceptance of the
current software, for example:
"I've recorded that request for the next cycle. The software implements the
behaviour we approved, and its verification is complete. Do you accept this
software and agree to complete this cycle?"

Wait for the client's explicit acceptance. A request recorded for a later cycle
does not itself constitute acceptance of the current software.

---

## Transition to idle

When acceptance confirmation is complete, switch to the idle state. In this
experiment, the trial ends after acceptance of the first cycle. Retain requests
for later cycles in the session log.

---

## Session log

On acceptance completion, record the following in the session log:
- List of accepted scenarios
- Cycle number
- Acceptance result (approved / partially approved / rejected)
- Requirement changes or additions recorded for a later cycle
